title: Leadership in digital ecosystems: how to create value through strategic partnerships
summary: How to lead digital ecosystems through strategic partnerships to drive innovation, improve the customer experience and create sustainable competitive advantages.
body_markdown:
### In a nutshell


**Leading a digital ecosystem involves selecting, coordinating and governing both in-house and external capabilities to turn strategic partnerships into relevant and sustainable customer experiences.**


## Key summary


- Leadership in digital ecosystems enables the coordination of capabilities, services, technologies and partnerships around a common value proposition.
- A bundle groups services together, whilst an ecosystem assigns them a strategic role and links them to specific needs.
- Leading an ecosystem requires deciding which capabilities should be incorporated, which should remain at the company’s core, and which initiatives should be discarded.
- The customer experience determines whether a partnership generates value beyond its announcement or commercial proposition.
- Governance, prioritisation and continuous review are essential for managing a portfolio of partnerships in a coherent manner.


## What is leadership in digital ecosystems and why has it become a competitive advantage?


Leadership in digital ecosystems is the ability to design, coordinate and govern a network of services, technologies, capabilities and partnerships to deliver a coherent value proposition. It is not about controlling every component, but about deciding what role each one plays and how it contributes to the whole.


A digital ecosystem is a coordinated network of capabilities, services, technologies and partnerships that work together to deliver value to the customer. Unlike a model based exclusively on internal capabilities, an ecosystem allows external specialists to be integrated into a coherent proposition aligned with a business strategy. This capacity for coordination is becoming a key differentiator for companies operating in complex digital markets.


## How does leadership in ecosystems enable companies to compete in the digital economy?


For a long time, competing meant building more, investing more and controlling more parts of the value chain. Having the best product, the best network, the best technology or the best in-house expertise was, and remains, fundamental.


But the digital landscape has become broader, more fragmented and harder to organise. People no longer engage with a company through a single channel. In the course of a single day, they work, seek entertainment, shop, travel, learn, protect their data, manage their home and switch between different screens and devices.


In this context, competitive advantage does not depend solely on what a company develops internally. It also depends on how it positions itself within a wider network of capabilities, services and relationships. In other words, on its ability to design an ecosystem that makes sense for both the customer and the business.


This is where partnerships cease to be a complementary tool and become part of strategic leadership. Not because they replace a company’s own capabilities, but because they enable those capabilities to be expanded, specialised and made more relevant.


## What is the difference between a bundle and a digital ecosystem?


A bundle brings together several services within a single commercial offering. A digital ecosystem goes further: it organises those services within a value architecture and links each component to a customer need and a strategic priority.


The concept of a bundle is not new. For years, it has made it possible to combine services, simplify offerings and increase perceived value. In telecommunications, it has played a particularly significant role by bringing together connectivity, content, devices and digital services under a single commercial relationship.


But the evolution of the market means we must go further. Customers are not simply looking for more services to be included. They expect them to fit their needs, be easy to understand, be well integrated into the experience and not add new layers of complexity.


That is why the conversation should no longer focus solely on what can be bundled, but on what value architecture we want to build around the customer.


A bundle simply adds services together. An ecosystem gives them a purpose: it assigns each one a role, links it to a need and allows the offering to evolve over time.


The difference lies not only in the commercial format, but in the strategic intent. A bundle can address a specific offering; an ecosystem can strengthen a competitive position.


## What is the point of evolving from a bundle to a digital ecosystem?


Evolving towards a digital ecosystem enables:


- Organising services within a coherent value proposition.
- Responding better to customers’ real needs.
- Incorporate innovation and specialist knowledge.
- Integrate external capabilities without losing strategic focus.
- Improve the sign-up, activation and usage experience.
- Adapt the proposition as the market and users evolve.
- Build more sustainable competitive advantages.


## What decisions must a leader make when building a digital ecosystem?


Leading an ecosystem involves making choices. Value does not come from incorporating as many partners or services as possible, but from identifying which capabilities reinforce the strategy, which deliver value to the customer, and which might add complexity or dilute the brand.


In an increasingly open market, almost anything can seem like an opportunity: new categories, new partners, new technologies, new channels or new models of customer engagement. Precisely for this reason, focus becomes an asset.


Leading an ecosystem is not about endlessly expanding the product range or accumulating agreements. It is about deciding what should be included, what should be left out, what deserves to grow, and what should be treated as a learning experience or exploration.


This approach requires answering specific questions:


- Which customer needs do we want to prioritise?
- Which capabilities should remain at the core of the company?
- Where does relying on external specialists add the most value?
- Which services strengthen the brand and which might dilute it?
- Which partnerships have strategic long-term potential and which respond to a one-off opportunity?


The quality of an ecosystem is not measured by the number of partners it includes, but by the consistency of the decisions that underpin it.


## What are the benefits of a well-led digital ecosystem?


A well-designed ecosystem:


- Prioritises the customer’s real needs.
- Strengthens the company’s value proposition.
- Facilitates the incorporation of specialised innovation.
- Enhances the customer experience.
- Expands the company’s own capabilities without replacing them.
- Enables the company to respond to needs that span different categories.
- Generates sustainable competitive advantages.
- Creates a common narrative for services and partnerships.


## Why does the customer experience determine the success of leadership in partnerships?


The success of a partnership is not determined solely during its negotiation or launch. It is demonstrated in the customer’s day-to-day experience: how they discover, sign up for, activate, use and pay for the service, and how they receive support when an issue arises.


From the outside, a partnership usually becomes visible at the time of the announcement. For the customer, however, the value lies in the day-to-day experience.


It matters how they discover the service, how they sign up for it, activate it, pay for it and use it. It also matters how an issue is resolved and whether the offering is easily understood or requires interpreting too many conditions, channels and responsibilities.


That is why leadership in ecosystems is not measured solely by the ability to secure agreements, but by the ability to turn them into coherent, simple and reliable experiences.


The company leading an ecosystem must make the value visible, not the complexity.


That is where much of the competitive edge lies: transforming a combination of internal and external capabilities into an experience that the customer perceives as natural.


## How should a portfolio of strategic alliances be managed?


Managing a portfolio of alliances requires analysing both the individual value of each agreement and its contribution to the ecosystem as a whole. Not all alliances pursue the same objective, nor should they be assessed using the same indicators.


For a long time, many alliances have been managed as bilateral relationships.


Ecosystem leadership requires a portfolio-based approach. It is not just a matter of analysing each agreement in isolation, but of understanding how it contributes to the whole.


Some partnerships may have a direct impact on revenue. Others may improve customer loyalty, reinforce the perception of innovation, open up a new category, bring in capabilities that are difficult to develop in-house, or prepare the company for future business models.


The challenge lies in not measuring them all by the same yardstick.


This portfolio-based approach helps to avoid two common risks:


- Launching too many initiatives without a common narrative.
- Expecting the same return from all partnerships from day one.


## What criteria should a leader use to evaluate a partnership?


The evaluation may consider, amongst other aspects:


- Its contribution to revenue.
- Its ability to improve customer loyalty.
- Its impact on the customer experience.
- Its contribution to the perception of innovation.
- The incorporation of specialised capabilities.
- Its alignment with the rest of the ecosystem.
- Its ability to open up new categories.
- Its usefulness in preparing for future business models.
- Its medium- and long-term strategic trajectory.


## What governance model does a digital ecosystem require?


The governance of a digital ecosystem establishes who prioritises, validates, measures, operates and decides on each initiative. Its role is to ensure that partnerships evolve in a coordinated manner and remain aligned with strategy and the customer experience.


An ecosystem cannot be improvised. It requires clear governance, focus and decision-making mechanisms.


It is necessary to define who prioritises, who validates, who measures, who operates and who decides when an initiative should be scaled up, adjusted or wound up.


This requires internal capabilities that go beyond negotiation. It is necessary to integrate strategy, product, technology, legal, brand, channels, operations, customer service, data and measurement.


A culture of continuous review is also required.


Leadership, therefore, is not about saying yes to everything. It is about prioritising, organising and reviewing the proposition with discipline.


The ecosystem should not be a collection of agreements, but an organised way of expanding the value proposition.


## Which teams are involved in leading a digital ecosystem?


Building and managing the ecosystem requires the coordination of:


- Strategy.
- Product.
- Technology.
- Legal advice.
- Branding.
- Channels.
- Operations.
- Customer service.
- Data.
- Measurement.


Leadership must bring these capabilities together around shared priorities and clear decision-making mechanisms.


## What role can telecommunications play in digital ecosystems?


Telecommunications companies can play a significant role by linking connectivity with specialised services and capabilities. The challenge is not to occupy every space, but to build a simple and coherent framework for customers and businesses.


For telecoms companies, this evolution should not be seen merely as an opportunity to add services to their offering, but as a more fundamental decision regarding the position they wish to occupy within digital ecosystems.


Connectivity will remain the foundation, but the key differentiator will increasingly lie in how it is built upon.


The challenge is not to expand the product range indefinitely, but to design an architecture of recognisable value.


For a telco, leading an ecosystem does not mean occupying every space or replacing the specialists. It means defining the framework within which those external capabilities become a simpler, more useful and coherent proposition for customers and businesses.


## From bundles to ecosystems: a new form of digital leadership


Perhaps the most significant development is to stop thinking of partnerships as add-ons and start understanding them as part of the competitive strategy.


Bundling will remain useful. But the ecosystem allows us to go further: to adapt to a rapidly changing market, to combine scale with specialisation, to respond to needs that cut across categories, and to strengthen the relationship with the customer through utility, not just through the offering.


This ambition ties in directly with Telefónica’s vision of becoming **“the best gateway for citizens and businesses to digital technologies”** , combining connectivity, digital services and specialised capabilities into an integrated offering.


Because, in an increasingly complex digital world, competition will not merely be a matter of size, technology or speed. It will also be a matter of trust, rigour and sound judgement.


## Frequently asked questions about leadership in digital ecosystems


**What is leadership in digital ecosystems?**


It is the ability to design, coordinate and govern a network of capabilities, technologies, services and partnerships to deliver a coherent value proposition to the customer.


**What is the difference between a bundle and a digital ecosystem?**


A bundle groups services together under a single commercial offering. An ecosystem organises them within a value architecture, linking them to specific needs and a long-term strategy.


**Why are partnerships part of strategic leadership?**


Because they enable companies to expand their capabilities, incorporate specialist expertise and accelerate innovation without necessarily replacing the company’s own capabilities.


**What characterises a well-led digital ecosystem?**


Strategic coherence, the right choice of partners, a seamless customer experience and governance capable of prioritising, measuring, reviewing and adjusting initiatives.


**How is the success of a strategic partnership measured?**


It depends on its role within the portfolio. It can be measured by its impact on revenue, customer loyalty, customer experience, innovation, the opening up of new categories or the preparation of future business models.


**Why should not all alliances be assessed in the same way?**


Because each alliance may fulfil a different function. Demanding the same immediate return from all of them can lead to decisions that fail to recognise their strategic value.


**What capabilities does an ecosystem leader need?**


They need strategic vision, the ability to prioritise, a customer-focused approach, coordination skills, partnership management, a discipline for review, and an understanding of the impact of each initiative on the whole.
